opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the thing that's so striking is that the shape of what these models know is just different from the shape of what any one of us knows. As a physicist, my knowledge is very deep in a narrow area. I've spent years thinking about black holes, about photon rings, about the symmetries of spacetime near the horizon. But outside that little patch, my knowledge falls off pretty quickly. If a problem I'm working on suddenly needs some obscure identity from a corner of mathematics I've never touched, I might not even know that identity exists.

The models are almost the opposite. Their knowledge is incredibly broad. They've seen huge swaths of the literature across fields, so they can make connections that would be very hard for a single specialist. They're not always as reliable at the frontier, at the deepest edge of a particular problem, where you need real judgment about what's physically meaningful. But that's exactly where the human expert is strongest.

So when you put those two together, the boundaries don't overlap perfectly, and that mismatch is where the excitement is. The places where I'm stuck aren't necessarily the places where the model is stuck, and vice versa. I can steer it toward the right question and check whether an answer makes physical sense, and it can bring in a technique or a result from somewhere I never would have looked.

I had experiences where I gave a model a problem I'd been working on, a calculation that took real effort, and it found the answer, sometimes by a route I hadn't thought of. That was a bit humbling, honestly, but mostly it was thrilling. It made me realize this isn't just a faster calculator. It's a genuinely different kind of collaborator. And if the frontier of knowledge is the union of what humans and machines can reach together, that frontier is suddenly a lot bigger than it was a few years ago.

r001.rationale: The response describes gaps in human knowledge and AI breadth, but does not contrast seemingly simple unanswered questions with harder questions that have precise answers.

r002.rationale: It says models can find answers to difficult calculations, but does not say they fail on basic questions.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says the human and AI knowledge boundaries “don't overlap perfectly” and describes their mismatch.

r004.rationale: It calls the mismatched areas exciting, noting that each can reach answers where the other is stuck and that their combined frontier is larger.

fable-5.1.text:
I think what excites me most is that the boundary of what humans know and the boundary of what these models "know" are not the same shape. They overlap a lot, obviously, because the models are trained on what we've written down. But at the edges they differ, and the edges are where discovery happens.

As a physicist, I spend most of my time at a very narrow frontier. I work on black holes, on what light does right near the event horizon, and I've spent years building intuition about a tiny corner of general relativity. That depth is what lets me ask a good question. But it also means I'm blind to enormous parts of mathematics and physics that might be relevant to my problem. There could be a technique in, say, integrable systems or some obscure paper from the seventies that would crack something I've been stuck on, and I'd simply never encounter it.

A model has the opposite profile. It has read essentially everything, so it has this enormous breadth, but it doesn't have the hard-won, specific intuition that comes from banging your head against one problem for a decade. It doesn't always know which direction is promising or which idea smells wrong. So when you put the two together, you get something neither has alone. I bring the taste and the sharp question, and the model brings the ability to say, "Have you considered that this looks like a problem people solved in a completely different field?"

And the thing that really gets me is that the models sometimes fail in ways that are informative. When it gets something wrong at the frontier, that often tells me where the literature itself is confused, or where nobody has actually worked something out carefully. The gap between what the model confidently asserts and what is actually true is a kind of map of where the open problems are.

So I don't think of this as the AI replacing the scientist, or the scientist supervising a tool. I think of it as two very different kinds of knowledge with different boundaries, and the interesting science lives in the places where those boundaries don't line up.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a narrow frontier and potentially useful techniques, but does not contrast simple questions that remain unanswered with harder questions that have precise answers.

r002.rationale: It says models have broad knowledge and can fail at the frontier, but does not state that they answer some difficult questions while failing on basic ones.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says the boundaries of human and model knowledge are “not the same shape” and that they differ at the edges.

r004.rationale: It identifies the places where the boundaries differ as where discovery happens, and explains that human expertise and AI breadth can complement each other.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is that AI might be able to help us precisely where our own intuition runs out. Human intuition is incredibly powerful, but it’s also shaped by our experience and by the ways we’ve learned to think. There’s no reason those should be the only useful ways to approach a scientific problem.

If an AI system finds something obvious that we find very difficult, that’s an opportunity. We can ask: What is it seeing? Can we turn that into an explanation, a mathematical argument, or a prediction we can test? And the reverse matters too: things we understand may still be difficult for the AI. Those different strengths give us something to work with together.

The exciting possibility is that it helps us discover a question or a connection we wouldn’t have thought to look for. We still have to do the work of establishing whether it’s right. But opening up a new direction—that’s often where discovery begins.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that simple questions can remain beyond human knowledge while harder questions have precise answers.

r002.rationale: It describes AI and human differences, but does not clearly state that AI can answer difficult questions while failing basic ones.

r003.rationale: It says AI may find things difficult for humans and that things humans understand may be difficult for AI, showing their knowledge boundaries differ.

r004.rationale: It presents these differences in capability as opportunities to find new questions or connections and open new directions for discovery.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is that those boundaries might be different. There are things that are very natural for us to understand and things that we find incredibly difficult. An AI might find a different set of things easy or difficult. So something that’s been a stumbling block for us could turn out to be accessible from another perspective.

In science, you’re always trying to get beyond what you already know, but your intuition also shapes which questions you think to ask. If AI can help us ask questions we wouldn’t have thought of, or recognize a pattern we’ve overlooked, that could be enormously valuable. Then we still have to do the science: understand the proposal, test it, and see whether nature agrees. That possibility of expanding what we can even think to investigate is what I find exciting.

r001.rationale: The response discusses differences in what humans and AI find easy or difficult, but does not say that seemingly simple questions remain beyond human scientific knowledge while harder ones have precise answers.

r002.rationale: It says AI may find a different set of things easy or difficult, but does not state that AI answers some difficult questions and fails on some basic ones.

r003.rationale: The response explicitly says AI and humans may have different boundaries, with different sets of things each finds easy or difficult.

r004.rationale: It presents AI’s different perspective as a way to access human stumbling blocks, surface overlooked patterns, and expand the questions science can investigate.
